title: Alcohol and Sleep Apnea: Why Drinking Makes Snoring Worse
excerpt: How alcohol relaxes your airway and worsens sleep apnea and snoring, what the research shows, how to drink more safely with CPAP, and when to get a sleep test.
metaDescription: How alcohol worsens sleep apnea and snoring by relaxing your airway, what the research says, CPAP tips, and when to see a doctor about a sleep test.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol and sleep apnea are a bad pairing. Alcohol relaxes the muscles that keep your throat open and slows the brain's alarm that wakes you when you stop breathing. If you already have obstructive sleep apnea, drinking in the evening usually makes the breathing pauses more frequent, longer, and harder on your oxygen levels. If you don't have it, a few drinks can still make you snore and, in some people, cause short pauses you'd never know about. The good news is that the effect depends heavily on timing and amount, so a few simple changes make a real difference.

**The quick rules:** Keep drinks earlier in the evening and give yourself a gap of three to four hours before bed. Have less on nights you know you'll sleep alone or without your CPAP nearby. Never skip your CPAP or oral appliance after drinking. Don't stack alcohol with sleeping pills, benzodiazepines, opioid painkillers, or sedating antihistamines. And if you snore loudly, gasp in your sleep, or feel exhausted during the day, get checked for sleep apnea, whether you drink or not.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article explains general research. It isn't a diagnosis and doesn't replace advice from a doctor who knows you. **Talk to your doctor or ask about a sleep study if** a partner has seen you stop breathing, gasp, or choke in your sleep; you snore loudly most nights, not just after drinking; you're sleepy enough during the day to doze off while reading, watching TV, or driving; you wake with headaches or a very dry mouth; or you have high blood pressure, heart rhythm problems, or type 2 diabetes along with heavy snoring. **Get help right away** if someone is very hard to wake after drinking, is breathing very slowly or irregularly, has blue or gray lips, or has taken alcohol together with opioids, sleeping pills, or benzodiazepines and seems over-sedated. Call 911 (or your local emergency number). That is an emergency, not a hangover.

## What Sleep Apnea Actually Is

Sleep apnea means your breathing repeatedly stops or becomes very shallow while you sleep. There are two main types.

- **Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA)** is by far the most common. Your brain keeps sending the signal to breathe, but your upper airway, the soft tube behind your tongue and at the back of your throat, collapses or narrows so air can't get through. Your chest heaves against a blocked pipe until your oxygen drops and your brain briefly jolts you toward waking to reopen it. Then you fall back asleep and the cycle starts again, sometimes dozens of times an hour.
- **Central sleep apnea** is less common. Here the brain itself pauses the signal to breathe. It's linked mostly to heart failure, stroke, high altitude, and opioid medicines.

When people talk about alcohol and sleep apnea, they almost always mean the obstructive kind, so that's the focus here.

Doctors measure severity with the **apnea-hypopnea index (AHI)**, which counts how many full pauses (apneas) and partial pauses (hypopneas) you have per hour of sleep. In adults, 5 to 14 an hour is usually called mild, 15 to 29 moderate, and 30 or more severe. Most people with OSA don't know they have it. They just know they snore, sleep badly, or feel tired.

## How Alcohol Affects Your Airway: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Your throat has no bone or cartilage holding it open the way your windpipe does. It stays open during sleep because a group of small muscles, including the main tongue muscle (the genioglossus), keep a little tension on it. Alcohol interferes with that system in a few ways at once.

### 1. It relaxes the muscles that hold your throat open

Alcohol is a depressant. It boosts the brain's main calming signal (GABA) and dampens its main excitatory signal (glutamate). That's why it relaxes you. Unfortunately, the same effect reaches the nerves that keep your airway muscles toned. Studies going back to the early 1980s found that alcohol selectively reduces activity in the tongue and throat muscles more than in the diaphragm, your main breathing muscle. So the diaphragm keeps pulling air in hard while the airway it's pulling through gets floppier. That mismatch is exactly what makes the airway suck shut.

### 2. It dulls the alarm that wakes you up

When your airway closes, the rising carbon dioxide and falling oxygen in your blood normally trigger a brief arousal. You don't fully wake, but your brain lifts out of deep sleep just enough to tighten the throat muscles and take a breath. Alcohol blunts that arousal response. The result is that each pause tends to go on longer before your brain reacts, and your oxygen level falls further during each one.

### 3. It changes the shape of your night

Alcohol makes you fall asleep faster and pushes you into deeper sleep in the first half of the night, while holding back REM (dreaming) sleep. As the alcohol wears off, REM comes back with a rebound in the second half. Obstructive sleep apnea is often worse during REM because your body's muscles are at their most relaxed then. Combined with the deep, heavily sedated sleep early on, it means alcohol can make both halves of the night rougher for your breathing. Our deeper explainer on [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) walks through the sleep-stage effects in detail.

### 4. It can stuff up your nose

Alcohol widens blood vessels, including those in the lining of the nose. Some drinks, especially red wine, also contain histamine and other compounds that can cause congestion in sensitive people. A blocked nose pushes you toward mouth-breathing, and mouth-breathing lets the jaw and tongue fall back, which narrows the airway further.

### 5. It makes back-sleeping more likely

People who've been drinking tend to sleep heavily in whatever position they land in, often on their back. Back-sleeping lets gravity pull the tongue and soft palate toward the back of the throat. For many people with OSA, the pauses are much more frequent on their back than on their side.

Put together, alcohol narrows the airway, makes it floppier, keeps you from reacting when it closes, and nudges you into the positions and sleep stages where apnea is worst.

## What the Research Says

This is one of the better-studied effects of alcohol on sleep, and the findings line up.

**Alcohol worsens existing sleep apnea.** Lab studies in which people with OSA sleep once sober and once after an evening dose of alcohol have consistently found more breathing pauses, longer pauses, and deeper drops in oxygen on the alcohol nights. The effect tends to be dose-dependent: more alcohol, closer to bed, means a bigger effect.

**Alcohol can bring out apnea in people who normally breathe fine.** Early sleep-lab studies in the 1980s found that a moderate evening dose of alcohol caused breathing pauses and oxygen dips in men who snored but didn't have apnea when sober, and even produced some events in people with no symptoms at all. These were small studies, but the pattern has held up.

**Regular drinking is linked to a higher risk of sleep apnea.** A 2018 systematic review and meta-analysis in the journal *Sleep Medicine* (Simou, Britton, and Leonardi-Bee) pooled data from many studies and found that higher alcohol consumption was associated with roughly a 25% higher risk of sleep apnea. That's an association, not proof that alcohol caused every case. Heavy drinking also tends to go with weight gain and poorer sleep habits, which are risk factors in their own right. But it's consistent with what the lab studies show about alcohol and the airway.

**Sleep specialists routinely advise limiting evening alcohol.** Avoiding alcohol in the hours before bed is standard advice from sleep medicine organizations and clinicians for people with OSA, alongside weight management and sleeping on your side.

## Snoring After Drinking: Why It Happens and What It Means

A lot of people search this topic because a partner told them they snore like a freight train after a few drinks but are quiet the rest of the time. That's a very common pattern, and it has the same cause as everything above.

Snoring is simply the sound of the soft palate, uvula, and tongue vibrating as air squeezes through a narrowed throat. Alcohol relaxes those tissues and narrows the passage, so air flows faster and more turbulently, and the tissues flutter. A stuffy nose and back-sleeping add to it.

What it means depends on the pattern:

- **You only snore after drinking, it's soft, and nobody's noticed pauses.** This is the most common and usually the least worrying. Your airway handles normal nights fine and alcohol tips it into snoring. Cutting back in the evening is often enough.
- **You snore after drinking and someone has heard you stop breathing, choke, or gasp.** That's a sign alcohol may be pushing you into actual apneas. It's worth mentioning to a doctor, especially if you drink on more than the occasional weekend.
- **You snore loudly most nights, and it's worse after drinking.** This is the pattern most likely to mean underlying sleep apnea. Alcohol isn't the root cause here, it's making an existing problem louder. Get assessed.

Snoring is also a good early warning. Airways that only collapse with alcohol today can become airways that collapse without it as people gain weight or get older. Paying attention now is easier than catching up later.

## How Alcohol and Sleep Apnea Feel the Next Morning

People with untreated apnea often feel worse after drinking than their friends do, and it's easy to blame it all on a hangover. Repeated breathing pauses fragment your sleep and drop your oxygen, and alcohol already lowers sleep quality on its own. The overlap can look like this:

- Waking up unrefreshed even after a long night in bed
- A dull morning headache that eases within an hour or two (common in apnea because of carbon dioxide build-up overnight)
- Very dry mouth and sore throat from mouth-breathing and snoring
- Waking several times to urinate (apnea itself increases nighttime urine, and alcohol adds to it)
- A pounding or racing heart during the night or on waking
- Grogginess, poor focus, and irritability through the day

Some of these are also classic hangover symptoms, so it's hard to tell them apart on any one morning. The clue is the pattern. If you feel noticeably worse after drinking than the amount would explain, or you feel this way on many mornings regardless of drinking, apnea may be part of the picture. If you often wake in the early hours after drinking, our guide to [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) covers the other reasons that happens, and [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) explains when a pounding heart is a reason to get checked.

## The Real Risks of Mixing Alcohol and Untreated Sleep Apnea

For someone with mild apnea that is diagnosed and treated, an occasional early drink is not usually an emergency. The risk climbs with how often you drink, how much, how close to bedtime, and how severe your apnea is. If your apnea is moderate or severe, untreated, or you also take sedating medicines, ask your sleep doctor whether you should drink at all.

**Drowsy driving.** Untreated sleep apnea is well known to raise the risk of car crashes because of daytime sleepiness. Alcohol the night before adds poorer sleep on top, and any alcohol still in your system the next morning adds impairment. If you feel sleepy behind the wheel, pull over.

**Heart and blood pressure strain.** Every apnea causes a surge in stress hormones and a spike in blood pressure as your body fights to breathe. Over years, untreated OSA is linked with high blood pressure, atrial fibrillation (an irregular heart rhythm), heart disease, and stroke. Heavy drinking independently raises blood pressure and atrial fibrillation risk. The two pile onto the same system.

**Deeper oxygen drops.** Because alcohol delays the arousal that ends each pause, oxygen levels can fall further than they would sober. For someone with severe apnea, or with lung or heart disease, that matters more.

**Combining alcohol with sedating medicines.** This is the one to take most seriously. Opioid painkillers, benzodiazepines (such as those used for anxiety), prescription sleeping pills, some muscle relaxants, and sedating antihistamines all slow breathing or blunt the urge to wake up. Adding alcohol multiplies that effect. With untreated sleep apnea in the mix, the combination can cause dangerous breathing problems during sleep. Never combine them without talking to your doctor or pharmacist first.

## Who Is Most at Risk

Alcohol makes any narrow airway worse, so the people who should be most careful are those who already have risk factors for obstructive sleep apnea:

- **Excess weight**, especially around the neck and upper body
- **A thick neck** (as a rough guide, often over 17 inches in men or 16 inches in women)
- **Being male**, though risk in women rises after menopause
- **Getting older**, as throat muscle tone declines
- **A small or set-back jaw, large tonsils, or a large tongue**
- **Chronic nasal congestion** from allergies or a deviated septum
- **Family history** of sleep apnea
- **Smoking**, which inflames and swells the airway
- **High blood pressure**, especially if it's hard to control

Doctors often use a short screening questionnaire called **STOP-BANG**, which asks about snoring, tiredness, observed pauses, blood pressure, body mass index, age, neck size, and sex. It's a screening tool, not a diagnosis, but scoring high on it is a good reason to ask for a sleep test.

## If You Have Sleep Apnea and Want to Drink: Practical Ways to Lower the Impact

You don't necessarily have to give up drinking entirely. These steps cut down how much alcohol affects your breathing at night.

1. **Front-load your evening.** Have your drinks earlier and stop at least three to four hours before bed. Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though it varies person to person, so the earlier you stop, the less alcohol is in your blood when you fall asleep.
2. **Keep the amount modest.** The effect on the airway grows with the dose. One or two drinks early is very different from five at midnight.
3. **Always use your treatment.** Put your CPAP mask on or your oral appliance in after drinking, even if you're tired and it feels like a hassle. Nights when you've been drinking are the nights you need it most.
4. **Sleep on your side.** If your apnea is worse on your back, use a body pillow, a backpack-style positional device, or a wedge to stay on your side.
5. **Clear your nose.** If drinking stuffs you up, a saline rinse or spray before bed can help. Ask a pharmacist about decongestants before using them, especially if you have high blood pressure.
6. **Don't mix with sedatives.** Skip sleeping pills, sedating antihistamines, and leftover painkillers on nights you drink unless your doctor has specifically said otherwise.
7. **Eat and hydrate.** A meal slows how quickly alcohol is absorbed, and water helps with the dry mouth that snoring and mouth-breathing cause.
8. **Don't use alcohol as a sleep aid.** It helps you drop off faster but makes the rest of the night worse, and that's doubly true with apnea. If you're tempted to have a nightcap because you sleep badly, the poor sleep itself is worth bringing to a doctor. Our piece on [why alcohol makes you sleepy](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-sleepy) explains why the drowsiness doesn't turn into good sleep.

## Alcohol and CPAP: What to Know

CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) works by blowing a steady stream of air through a mask to splint your throat open. It's the most effective standard treatment for moderate and severe OSA.

Alcohol makes the airway more collapsible, so in theory it can take a bit more pressure to keep it open on drinking nights. Research on how much this matters in practice is mixed, and many people find their usual settings still work fine after a moderate amount. Some people notice more mask leaks or more mouth-breathing after drinking, which can make a nasal mask less effective. Auto-adjusting CPAP machines respond to changes in pressure needs during the night, which can help on those nights.

The practical message is simple: wear it every time, and if you drink regularly, tell your sleep doctor. Your machine's data may show whether your breathing events go up on drinking nights, and they can adjust your settings or mask if needed.

Other treatments include oral appliances that pull the lower jaw forward, positional therapy, a surgically implanted nerve stimulator for some people who can't use CPAP, and weight loss. In late 2024 the FDA approved tirzepatide (sold as Zepbound) for moderate to severe OSA in adults with obesity, the first medicine approved for the condition. All of these work better if alcohol isn't fighting them every evening.

## How Sleep Apnea Is Diagnosed

If any of this sounds familiar, the next step is simple. Your primary care doctor can screen you and refer you for a sleep study.

- **Home sleep apnea test.** You wear a small device overnight in your own bed that tracks your breathing, airflow, and blood oxygen. It's convenient and suitable for many adults suspected of having moderate to severe OSA.
- **In-lab sleep study (polysomnography).** You sleep overnight at a sleep center while sensors record your brain waves, breathing, oxygen, heart rhythm, and movements. It's more detailed and is used when the picture is less clear or other sleep disorders are possible.

Be honest with your doctor about how much and how late you usually drink. It helps them interpret your results, and some doctors may ask you to avoid alcohol on the test night so they see your baseline.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Since this is a site about hangovers, it's worth being direct: **there is no good evidence that DHM helps with sleep apnea or snoring**, and it is not a treatment for either. Nothing you take before or after drinking will stop alcohol from relaxing your airway. The steps that genuinely help are drinking less and earlier, sleeping on your side, and using your prescribed treatment.

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that has been studied for how it affects alcohol's action on the brain and for its role in alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms. Most of that research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. Some social drinkers use it on nights out to feel better the next morning. If that's you, it can sit alongside the habits above, never in place of them, and it doesn't make it safe to skip your CPAP. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when. If you have sleep apnea or take other medicines, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

For more on drinking in a way that's kinder to your sleep, see our guide to [sleep optimization for social drinkers](/never-hungover/sleep-optimization-social-drinkers-circadian-rhythm) and our overview of [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

Alcohol relaxes your throat muscles, slows your brain's response to breathing pauses, and pushes you into the sleep positions and stages where apnea is worst. That's why it makes snoring louder and obstructive sleep apnea more severe, and why it can cause some pauses even in people who normally breathe fine. The effect is driven by how much you drink and how close to bed. If you have sleep apnea, keep drinks modest and early, never skip your CPAP, and never combine alcohol with sedating medicines. If you snore heavily, gasp in your sleep, or feel worn out during the day, ask your doctor about a sleep test. It's a common, treatable condition, and sorting it out tends to improve both your nights and your mornings.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does alcohol make sleep apnea worse?**

Yes. Alcohol relaxes the muscles that hold your throat open and dulls the brain's reflex to wake you when breathing stops. In people who already have obstructive sleep apnea, drinking in the evening tends to make breathing pauses more frequent, last longer, and cause deeper drops in blood oxygen. The effect is strongest when you drink close to bedtime and when you drink more.

**Can alcohol cause sleep apnea in someone who doesn't have it?**

Alcohol can trigger snoring and some breathing pauses in people who normally breathe fine at night, especially after several drinks close to bed. Research pooling many studies has also linked regular drinking with a higher risk of having sleep apnea overall. That doesn't mean one night out gives you a lasting disorder, but if you only snore or gasp after drinking, it can be an early sign that your airway is on the narrow side.

**Why do I snore only when I drink?**

Snoring is the sound of soft tissue in your throat vibrating as air squeezes past it. Alcohol relaxes the tongue and throat muscles, makes you sleep more deeply in the first part of the night, and can stuff up your nose, so air has to push through a narrower, floppier passage. Sleeping on your back after drinking makes it worse because gravity pulls the tongue backward.

**How long before bed should I stop drinking if I have sleep apnea?**

There is no single official cut-off, but a common recommendation from sleep specialists is to avoid alcohol for at least three to four hours before bed, and to keep the amount small. The less alcohol still in your blood when you fall asleep, the less it relaxes your airway. Ask your sleep doctor what they recommend for your situation.

**Is it safe to drink alcohol if I use a CPAP machine?**

Many people who use CPAP have an occasional drink, but alcohol can make your airway more collapsible, and some people find their usual pressure feels less effective or their mask leaks more after drinking. The most important rule is to always use your CPAP after drinking, never skip it. If you drink regularly, tell your sleep doctor so they can check your settings.

**Is mixing alcohol with sleeping pills dangerous if I have sleep apnea?**

It can be. Alcohol, sleeping pills, benzodiazepines, opioid painkillers, and some sedating antihistamines all slow breathing or blunt the urge to wake up when oxygen drops. Combining them on top of untreated sleep apnea raises the risk of dangerous breathing problems during sleep. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining any sedating medicine with alcohol.

**What are the signs of sleep apnea?**

The most common signs are loud, regular snoring, a partner noticing you stop breathing or gasp and choke in your sleep, waking with a dry mouth or headache, feeling tired or dozing off during the day even after a full night in bed, and waking several times a night to urinate. High blood pressure that is hard to control is another clue. If several of these sound familiar, ask your doctor about a sleep test.

**Does DHM help with sleep apnea?**

There is no good evidence that DHM helps with sleep apnea or snoring, and it is not a treatment for either. DHM has been studied mainly for how it affects alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms, mostly in animals. If you have sleep apnea, the steps that matter are drinking less in the evening, using your prescribed treatment, and working with your doctor.
